C005.subject: Higher minimum wages in low-wage labor markets with high employer concentration
C005.object: the number of independent fast-food operators that survive beyond 12 months
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Higher minimum wages in low-wage labor markets with high employer concentration the number of independent fast-food operators that survive beyond 12 months]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal administrative payroll data (e.g., from state unemployment insurance records) linked to business registration records for fast-food establishments in metropolitan areas with high employer concentration (e.g., using HHI thresholds > 2500) before and after a minimum wage increase — Provides direct, high-frequency evidence on survival rates of independent operators (single-unit vs. multi-unit) over 12-24 months, controlling for local economic conditions and chain competition.

[PATH:empirical] Survey or qualitative case studies of independent fast-food operators in low-wage markets with monopsonistic labor structures, focusing on their margin adjustments (e.g., price increases, hours reduction, owner labor) following a minimum wage hike — Captures the micro-level decision-making and non-labor cost responses that mediate survival, which administrative data may miss, and helps distinguish between temporary closure and permanent exit.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of monopsonistic competition and firm dynamics (e.g., search-and-matching models with heterogeneous firms) parameterized to simulate the effect of minimum wage increases on the equilibrium number of single-unit fast-food firms — Provides a causal framework to isolate the mechanism (profit squeeze vs. reduced labor turnover) and generate testable predictions about how market concentration moderates the survival effect, guiding empirical design.

qualifier.geographic: low-wage labor markets with high employer concentration

C006.object: the market share of large fast-food chains relative to independent operators

[PATH:empirical] Quarterly Workforce Indicators (QWI) data matched with fast-food establishment employment and market share data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) or private datasets like NPD Group — This would allow a difference-in-differences or event-study analysis comparing changes in market share of large chains vs. independent operators in high-concentration low-wage labor markets before and after minimum wage increases, controlling for local economic conditions.

[PATH:empirical] Survey or case-study evidence from independent fast-food operators in high-concentration markets (e.g., interviews or small business data from the Federal Reserve Small Business Credit Survey) — Directly assesses how independent operators respond to minimum wage hikes—whether they exit, reduce hours, or lose market share—providing micro-level evidence on the hypothesized competitive disadvantage.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of monopsonistic labor markets with differentiated products (e.g., Bhaskar, Manning & To, 2002; Azar, Marinescu & Steinbaum, 2022) — Provides a framework to predict that minimum wage increases in concentrated labor markets may reduce large firms' market share if independent operators are more labor-intensive or have less monopsony power, helping interpret empirical findings and identify mechanisms.

qualifier.geographic: low-wage labor markets with high employer concentration

[PATH:empirical] Qualitative case studies or surveys of independent fast-food operators in high-concentration markets (e.g., rural or urban low-wage areas) before and after minimum wage hikes. — Captures decision-making processes and motivations for conversion, providing causal mechanism evidence that complements quantitative analysis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of firm organizational choice under labor cost shocks and monopsony power (e.g., extensions of the Melitz or monopsony models to franchise vs. independent ownership). — Formalizes the hypothesized link and identifies conditions (e.g., degree of concentration, brand value) under which the effect should hold or reverse, guiding empirical design.

[PATH:empirical] Panel data from the National Establishment Time Series (NETS) or similar longitudinal business registry, combined with state minimum wage histories and local labor market concentration measures — Enables tracking of firm entry, exit, and growth dynamics to test whether minimum wage hikes disproportionately benefit large chains due to scale economies or financing advantages, conditional on weak employer wage coordination.
